extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, in-house counsel, patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether prior art references or prior acts anticipate patent claims (novelty/Section 102 issues), including anticipation by lists/ranges, Section 102(g)(2) prior making, and inherent anticipation. Summarizes Federal Circuit case law and how to apply those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art anticipates a patent claim when a single reference exhibits or discloses all limitations of the claim in the same arrangement or combination as the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation turns on disclosure of every limitation arranged as claimed; novelty is denied when the claimed subject matter is already known or disclosed to the public. (General statement appearing throughout the newsletter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by disclosure of components (combination must be immediately apparent)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior reference lists components of an invention, anticipation of a claimed combination depends on whether the particular combination would be "immediately apparent to one of ordinary skill" given the number and type of categories/components disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrigley v. Cadbury: a reference that specifically discloses menthol as a flavoring agent and WS-23 as a cooling agent (each in amounts within claimed ranges) supported anticipation because one skilled in the art would view using both in a single product as envisioned. Contrast with Impax Labs where picking components from long lists and experimenting with amounts did not anticipate. Consider: number of categories, specificity of listings, whether components are identified as preferred/nonessential, and whether the art links components to the claimed use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity, scope, and content of lists control whether listing anticipates combinations (Judge Newman view)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere listing of ingredients is not automatically a disclosure of their combination; whether a list discloses specific combinations depends on the scope, specificity, and content of the lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Newman (concurring/dissenting in Wrigley) cautioned that short/selective lists may warrant inference of known combinations but long lists (many categories, millions of combinations) are insufficient. Evaluate how selective the list is and whether it warrants an inference that particular combinations were known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus vs species / narrow range vs broad range
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a genus or a broad numerical range is not necessarily a disclosure of every species or every narrower subrange, but a broad numerical range may anticipate a narrower range under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClearValue v. Pearl River Polymers: a prior art disclosure of alkalinity up to 150 ppm anticipated a claimed ≤50 ppm limitation when there was no evidence the narrower range was 'critical' or that the claimed process worked differently within the broader range, and the prior art provided examples throughout the broader range. Atofina (distinguished) applied where the patentee had shown that the narrow range was critical to enabling the invention. When assessing range anticipation, look for evidence that the narrow range is critical or that the prior art enables the narrower portion of the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement for anticipation (practice without undue experimentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate, the reference must disclose the invention and enable one of ordinary skill to practice an embodiment without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference enables practicing the claimed embodiment across the disclosed range (with examples), it may anticipate. Testimony that the prior art 'taught away' is relevant to obviousness but not to anticipation. Focus on whether the prior reference provides sufficient enabling disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away is irrelevant to anticipation (but relevant to obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures that teach away from an invention may be relevant to an obviousness analysis but are inapplicable to anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClearValue: district court erred in giving weight to testimony that the prior art taught away when deciding anticipation. Separate analyses: anticipation looks only to whether the invention is disclosed and enabled; teaching away bears on obviousness inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 102(g)(2) prior making — conception/reduction-to-practice/diligence standards
rubrics_metrics.description: To invalidate a patent under Section 102(g)(2) for prior making in the U.S. by another, prior invention can be shown by earlier reduction to practice or by earlier conception coupled with reasonable diligence to reduce to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva v. AstraZeneca: the prior inventor need not appreciate the patentable feature or understand exactly how it works; it is sufficient to have conceived the invention and exercised reasonable diligence, or actually reduced it to practice first. Evaluate evidence of dates, conception, reduction to practice, and diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation of patented features not required for prior invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior inventor need not have appreciated that a particular feature was the reason for a result or have characterized the invention in the same words the patentee later uses in claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teva: the defendants had made a stable formulation and need not have understood crospovidone was the stabilizer to show prior invention; 'the invention is not the language of the claim but the subject matter thereby defined.' Do not require contemporaneous recognition of patentable significance to prove prior making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-written (oral) disclosures in the U.S. can constitute 'making the invention in this country'
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se requirement that a domestic disclosure be in writing; an oral disclosure in the U.S. can constitute prior making if it is specific enough to establish conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amkor v. ITC: oral communications of a foreign-made invention to persons in the U.S. can be sufficient, provided the disclosure is 'specific enough to encompass the complete and operative invention' and its contents can later be proven (e.g., by testimony). When assessing alleged oral disclosures, examine specificity, witnesses, and timing. Also account for burden-of-proof rules when date ranges overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and date-range rules in priority contests
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting invalidity (respondent) bears the burden of proving prior invention by clear and convincing evidence; rules about assigning conception dates within ranges apply differently depending on who bears the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amkor discussion: administrative/interference cases applied a rule that a party proving conception only within a range is deemed to have conceived at the end of that range, but the Federal Circuit limited application of that rule where the respondent (charging invalidity) bears the burden. Consider which party bears the burden when resolving overlapping date ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent anticipation — necessity/inevitability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference may anticipate inherently if all claim limitations are 'necessarily present, or inherent' in the reference even if not expressly stated; inherency requires that the missing characteristic inevitably flows from practicing the disclosed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montgomery: court found efficacy limitation inherent because administration of an RAS inhibitor to at-risk subjects inevitably treated or prevented stroke (court skeptical whether claims required efficacy but held inherency satisfied). Dissent (Lourie) emphasized that inherency requires inevitability and that an 'invitation to investigate' is not an inherent disclosure. Evaluate whether the allegedly inherent feature necessarily follows from the disclosure or is merely a possible/unproven result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim limitations are not inherent from mere structural disclosures unless the structure necessarily performs the function
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior structural disclosure does not inherently anticipate a claim recited in functional terms unless the prior structure necessarily performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bettcher Indus. v. Bunzl: prior blades with chamfers did not necessarily have 'bearing surfaces' just because chamfers existed; defendant failed to show more than a possibility that chamfers could perform bearing function. Courts will not transform one disclosed structure into a different claimed structure based on hypothetical surrounding configurations not disclosed. Look for evidence that the structure in the reference necessarily produced the claimed function.
